paper_metadata.title: Uncertainty and symmetry bounds for the quantum total detection probability

experiments.description: Analytical and illustrative quantum-walk detection on finite graphs using repeated projective measurements, with bounds and exact results evaluated on small graph instances such as rings and hypercubes.

algorithm.variant: stroboscopic quantum walk with repeated projective detection; dark/bright subspace analysis

hyperparameters.Hamiltonian_choice: adjacency matrix for standard quantum walk on graphs

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Particle occupies graph nodes; initial state |psi_in> and detection state |d> are states in the node basis.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Total detection probability P_det = sum_n |phi_n|^2 under repeated measurements until first successful detection.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Projective measurement with collapse postulate; unsuccessful detections renormalize the state and evolution continues.
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: H = A, the graph adjacency matrix for the standard quantum walk

problem_instance.description: Generic finite graph quantum-walk search/detection problem; examples analyzed include an even ring and the B-dimensional hypercube.

dataset_specification.description: Graph instances are theoretical: ring with L sites and hypercube with B bits; initial states are localized nodes or symmetric superpositions; detection on a chosen node or uniform ground state.

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Analytical derivation; comparison of lower bound, symmetry upper bound, and exact solution; illustrative figures for small systems and large hypercube scaling.

speedup_claims.conditions: paper studies bounds and exact values for quantum detection probability; classical baseline is always unity
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper does not claim an algorithmic speedup; it emphasizes that quantum detection can be less than unity due to dark states, unlike the classical case.

scalability_data.problem_size: ring with L sites (even L; examples include localized states at distance ξ< L/2)
